blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: This tree follows the topics and the problem list of NeetCode's roadmap (the NeetCode 150), with a learning page written for this site for each topic. The explanations and Java templates are ours; the problems belong to LeetCode, and each one links to its LeetCode page.

A **heap** keeps the smallest (min-heap) or largest (max-heap) element available in O(1) and lets you insert or remove it in O(log n). It does *not* keep everything sorted: it only guarantees the top. That is exactly enough for problems that repeatedly ask for "the best remaining item".

| Pattern | Idea | Problems |
|---|---|---|
| **Top K** | Keep a heap of size k; the heap root is the k-th best so far | Kth Largest in a Stream, K Closest Points, Kth Largest Element |
| **Two heaps** | A max-heap for the lower half and a min-heap for the upper half; the median sits at the tops | Find Median from Data Stream |
| **Scheduling / simulation** | Always take the next most urgent item | Task Scheduler, Last Stone Weight, Design Twitter |
| **Merge k sources** | Heap holds the current head of each source | Merge k Sorted Lists |

For "the k largest", use a **min-heap** of size k. When it overflows, you evict the smallest of your candidates. The heap then always holds the k largest seen so far, and its root is the k-th largest. Cost: O(n log k), better than sorting when k is small.
blocks.title: Counter-intuitive but true

blocks.text: `PriorityQueue<E>` is a **min-heap** by default. For a max-heap pass `Comparator.reverseOrder()` or a lambda. Its operations: `offer`/`add` O(log n), `poll` O(log n), `peek` O(1), `remove(Object)` O(n).

blocks.title: HeapTemplates.java

blocks.text: **What to notice.** `kClosest` compares **squared** distances, which keeps everything in integers and preserves the order. The two-heap `addNum` always pushes through `low` then `high`, which re-balances automatically with two lines instead of a tangle of `if`s.

- **Comparator overflow.** `(a, b) -> a - b` can overflow for large or negative values. Use `Integer.compare(a, b)`.
- **Iterating a `PriorityQueue`** does **not** give sorted order: only `poll()` does. `toString` and the for-each loop show the internal array.
- **`remove(Object)` is O(n).** If you need to delete arbitrary items often, use lazy deletion (skip stale entries when they reach the top) or a `TreeMap`.
- **Min versus max confusion** for top-K: the heap type is the *opposite* of the answer you want.
- **Ties.** If equal keys need a rule, put it in the comparator.

Bulk heap construction (heapify) sifts down from the middle of the array, and most nodes are near the bottom where sifting is cheap, which sums to O(n). Repeated insertion sifts each new element up through up to log n levels. Java's `PriorityQueue(Collection)` constructor uses the linear heapify.
blocks.title: Interview angle: Why is building a heap from n elements O(n), but inserting n elements one at a time O(n log n)?
Key points
blocks.text:
- A heap gives the best element in O(1) and removal or insertion in O(log n), but does not keep order
- Top K largest: min-heap of size k, top K smallest: max-heap of size k, O(n log k)
- Two heaps (max-heap low, min-heap high) maintain a running median
- `PriorityQueue` is a min-heap by default; reverse with `Comparator.reverseOrder()`
- Use `Integer.compare`, not subtraction
- Iterating a `PriorityQueue` is not sorted; `remove(Object)` is O(n)

blocks.text: Open **Practice** in the top bar and choose **Heap / Priority Queue** (under DSA by topic) to tick problems off, keep notes on each one, and add problems of your own.

items.question: How do you find the k-th largest element in a stream of numbers?
items.answer: Keep a min-heap of the k largest numbers. For each new number, add it and, if the size exceeds k, remove the smallest. The heap's root is the k-th largest. Each update costs O(log k).

items.question: When is a heap better than sorting?
items.answer: When you need only the top k of many items or a running best of a stream. A heap costs O(n log k) and O(k) space; sorting costs O(n log n) and needs all data first.

items.question: Why do you need two heaps to maintain a median?
items.answer: The median is at the boundary between the lower and upper halves of the data. A max-heap of the lower half and a min-heap of the upper half expose both boundary elements at their tops in O(1), and rebalancing keeps the sizes within one.
